subject: Preflight Preparation - Airworthiness Requirements
learning_objective: Determine required inspection intervals for aircraft equipment (transponder).
question_text: Maintenance records show the last transponder inspection was performed on September 1, 2014. The next inspection will be due no later than
explanation: Transponder tests/inspections are required every 24 calendar months (14 CFR 91.413). A calendar-month requirement runs to the end of the 24th month after the month of the last inspection, so from September 2014 the next inspection is due by the end of September 2016.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This applies a 12-month, not 24-month, interval.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This uses the exact anniversary date rather than the 'end of the 24th calendar month' rule, which extends to the end of that month.

calculation_steps: 24 calendar months from September 2014 = due by the end of September 2016.

choices.label: C

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 'Single-engine/multiengine land/sea' describes 'class,' a finer subdivision within the airplane category, not 'category' itself.

explanation: Per the 14 CFR 91.155 VFR weather minimums table, day VFR flight outside controlled airspace above 1,200 ft AGL and below 10,000 ft MSL requires 1 statute mile flight visibility.

explanation: In this altitude band (day or night), the 14 CFR 91.155 cloud clearance requirement outside controlled airspace is 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds; the minimum distance below clouds is therefore 500 feet.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Airworthiness Requirements
learning_objective: Calculate the next 100-hour inspection due time when the previous inspection was completed after the 100-hour point using the permitted 10-hour overrun.
question_text: A 100-hour inspection was due at 3302.5 hours. The 100-hour inspection was actually done at 3309.5 hours. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
explanation: The 100-hour inspection interval may be exceeded by up to 10 hours while en route to a place where it can be performed, but that excess time is counted toward the next 100-hour interval, which is computed from the time the inspection was originally due, not from when it was actually completed.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 3312.5 incorrectly adds only 10 hours to the actual completion time rather than computing a full 100-hour interval from the original due point.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 3395.5 incorrectly computes the next interval from the actual completion time (3309.5) using something other than a straightforward +100 hours.

regulation_reference: 14 CFR 91.409(b) (100-hour inspection requirement and the 10-hour overrun allowance).
calculation_steps: Original due point = 3302.5 hours. Next 100-hour inspection = 3302.5 + 100 = 3402.5 hours (the 7-hour overrun used to reach the inspection is counted against, not added on top of, the next interval).

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Frost/Icing Hazards)
learning_objective: Explain why frost is hazardous to flight.
question_text: Why is frost considered hazardous to flight?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frost changes the basic aerodynamic shape of the airfoils, thereby increasing lift.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frost slows the airflow over the airfoils, thereby increasing control effectiveness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frost spoils the smooth flow of air over the wings, thereby decreasing lifting capability.

explanation: Even a thin layer of frost disrupts the smooth airflow over the wing's upper surface, degrading lift and increasing stall speed, without necessarily being visible from the cockpit.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Frost decreases, not increases, effective lift.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Frost degrades, not increases, control effectiveness by disrupting airflow.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), icing/frost hazards.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Thunderstorms)
learning_objective: Identify the onset of the mature stage of a thunderstorm.
question_text: The mature stage of a thunderstorm begins with
explanation: The thunderstorm life cycle progresses through cumulus, mature, and dissipating stages; the mature stage begins when precipitation starts reaching the surface, marking the point at which both updrafts and downdrafts coexist.

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Continuous downdrafts dominate the dissipating stage, not the beginning of the mature stage.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Aircraft Systems (Flaps)
learning_objective: State a purpose of wing flaps.
question_text: What is one purpose of wing flaps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To enable the pilot to make steeper approaches to a landing without increasing the airspeed.

choices.label: B

subject: Emergency Operations - Engine Systems (Carburetor Icing)
learning_objective: Compare carburetor icing susceptibility between float-type carburetors and fuel injection systems.
question_text: With regard to carburetor ice, float-type carburetor systems in comparison to fuel injection systems are generally considered to be
explanation: Float-type carburetors are generally more susceptible to icing than fuel injection systems, because the venturi effect in the carburetor throat causes significant cooling that fuel-injected induction systems do not experience in the same way.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The two systems are not equally susceptible; float carburetors are notably more prone to icing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Float carburetors are more, not less, susceptible compared to fuel injection.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), induction systems.

learning_objective: Define angle of attack.

subject: Navigation - VOR Systems
learning_objective: Interpret CDI/OBS/TO-FROM indications during a VOR test signal (VOT) ground check.
question_text: When the course deviation indicator (CDI) needle is centered using a VOR test signal (VOT), the omnibearing selector (OBS) and the TO/FROM indicator should read

choices.label: A
choices.text: 180° FROM, only if the pilot is due north of the VOT.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0° TO or 180° FROM, regardless of the pilot`s position from the VOT.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0° FROM or 180° TO, regardless of the pilot`s position from the VOT.

explanation: A correctly functioning VOT check centers the CDI with the OBS reading 0° and a FROM indication, or 180° with a TO indication — regardless of the receiver's actual position, because a VOT signal simulates the 360° radial in all directions equally.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The correct VOT indication does not depend on the pilot's position relative to the station; it is the same anywhere within reception range.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This reverses the correct pairing of readings (0°/TO and 180°/FROM instead of the correct 0°/FROM and 180°/TO).

subject: Preflight Preparation - Aeronautical Decision-Making
learning_objective: Apply sound aeronautical decision-making to a marginal short-field takeoff performance scenario.
question_text: A pilot and two passengers landed on a 2,100 foot east-west gravel strip with an elevation of 1,800 feet. The temperature is warmer than expected and after computing the density altitude it is determined the takeoff distance over a 50 foot obstacle is 1,980 feet. The airplane is 75 pounds under gross weight. What would be the best choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Taking off into the headwind will give the extra climb-out time needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Try a takeoff without the passengers to make sure the climb is adequate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wait until the temperature decreases, and recalculate the takeoff performance.

explanation: With only about 120 feet of margin between required and available distance on a marginal gravel strip, the conservative, sound aeronautical-decision-making choice is to wait for cooler temperatures (which lower density altitude and shorten required takeoff distance) and recompute performance, rather than accept a thin safety margin.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Relying on an assumed headwind is not a verified performance margin and is not a sound substitute for recalculating under safer conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Removing passengers changes the loading and social situation without addressing the underlying issue in a verified, planned way; waiting for better conditions is the safer, more deliberate choice tested here.

regulation_reference: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) principles as taught in FAA guidance material.
handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-2 (Risk Management Handbook) / FAA-H-8083-25, aeronautical decision-making.
source_title: PAR - Private Pilot Airplane sample questions
copyright_status: U.S. Government work, public domain under 17 U.S.C. §105. Correct answer independently determined by this project — see question 1 note. This is a judgment-based ADM scenario; flagged for instructor review given the absence of an official answer key.

subject: Emergency Operations - Engine Systems (Carburetor Icing)
learning_objective: State the first indication of carburetor icing in a fixed-pitch-propeller, float-carburetor airplane.
question_text: If an aircraft is equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller and a float-type carburetor, the first indication of carburetor ice would most likely be

choices.label: A
choices.text: a drop in oil temperature and cylinder head temperature.

explanation: With a fixed-pitch propeller, engine power output is directly reflected in RPM, so the first indication of carburetor icing is typically a gradual loss of RPM (in a constant-speed-propeller aircraft, the first indication is instead a drop in manifold pressure, since RPM is held constant by the governor).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A drop in oil/cylinder head temperature is not the primary or earliest indicator of carburetor icing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Engine roughness tends to appear later, as icing becomes more severe, rather than being the first indication.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25 (Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge), induction icing.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (Aerodynamics)
learning_objective: Identify the statement that relates to Bernoulli's principle of lift.
question_text: Which statement relates to Bernoulli's principle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An additional upward force is generated as the lower surface of the airfoil deflects air downward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Air traveling faster over the curved upper surface of an airfoil causes lower pressure on the top surface.

explanation: Bernoulli's principle relates increased airflow speed over the curved upper surface of an airfoil to a corresponding decrease in pressure there, contributing to lift.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is Newton's third law, not Bernoulli's principle.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This describes the Newtonian reaction (downwash) explanation of lift, not Bernoulli's pressure-based principle.

subject: Emergency Operations - Emergency Approach
learning_objective: Explain the importance of maintaining a constant glide speed during an emergency approach.
question_text: When executing an emergency approach to land in a single-engine airplane, it is important to maintain a constant glide speed because variations in glide speed will

choices.label: A
choices.text: increase the chances of shock cooling the engine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: assure the proper descent angle is maintained until entering the flare.

choices.label: C
choices.text: nullify all attempts at accuracy in judgment of gliding distance and landing spot.

explanation: A constant best-glide speed is essential because varying glide speed changes the glide ratio, making it very difficult to accurately judge gliding distance and consistently reach the intended landing spot.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Shock cooling relates to rapid power/temperature changes, not the reason for maintaining constant glide speed for distance judgment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Maintaining descent angle 'until the flare' is not the specific reasoning being tested — the key issue is glide-distance/landing-spot accuracy.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-3 (Airplane Flying Handbook), emergency approach and landing.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Cross-Country Flight Planning
learning_objective: Calculate distance travelled given ground speed and time.
question_text: How far will an aircraft travel in 7.5 minutes with a ground speed of 114 knots?
explanation: Distance equals ground speed multiplied by time (in hours).

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 15.00 NM does not match the exact product of 114 kt x 0.125 hr.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 14.50 NM does not match the exact product of 114 kt x 0.125 hr.

calculation_steps: Time = 7.5 minutes = 7.5/60 = 0.125 hours. Distance = 114 kt x 0.125 hr = 14.25 NM.

subject: Navigation - GPS/RAIM

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: the pilot has no assurance of the accuracy of the GPS position.

choices.label: C

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Wind)
learning_objective: Explain why surface wind direction differs from wind direction aloft.
question_text: The wind at 5,000 feet AGL is southwesterly while the surface wind is southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to

choices.label: A
choices.text: stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: friction between the wind and the surface.

choices.label: C
choices.text: stronger Coriolis force at the surface.

explanation: Surface friction slows the wind and backs its direction relative to the gradient wind aloft, which is why surface wind direction differs (backed) from the wind direction at 5,000 feet AGL.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Pressure gradient strength is not the primary cause of this specific direction shift with height near the surface.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Coriolis force is weaker, not stronger, near the surface due to the counteracting effect of friction; friction (not Coriolis) explains the backing.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Weather (Temperature Inversion)
learning_objective: Describe the visibility conditions typically associated with a temperature inversion.
question_text: When there is a temperature inversion, you would expect to experience

choices.label: A
choices.text: clouds with extensive vertical development above an inversion aloft.

choices.label: B
choices.text: good visibility in the lower levels of the atmosphere and poor visibility above an inversion aloft.

choices.label: C
choices.text: an increase in temperature as altitude increases.

explanation: By definition, a temperature inversion is a layer in which temperature increases with height rather than decreasing, which tends to trap haze, smoke, and moisture near the surface, degrading visibility below the inversion.

subject: Preflight Preparation - Performance and Limitations (Density Altitude)
learning_objective: Determine the change in density altitude resulting from a temperature increase at a constant pressure altitude.
question_text: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8.) What is the effect of a temperature increase from 35 to 50°F on the density altitude if the pressure altitude remains at 3,000 feet MSL?
explanation: Reading the Density Altitude Chart (Figure 8) at 3,000 ft pressure altitude, density altitude increases by approximately 1,000 feet as temperature rises from 35°F to 50°F, since warmer air is less dense.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Density altitude increases (not decreases) with a temperature rise.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 1,300 feet overstates the increase shown on the chart/by calculation for this specific temperature change.

handbook_reference: FAA-CT-8080-2H, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement, Figure 8 (Density Altitude Chart).
calculation_steps: Using the density-altitude approximation (ISA deviation x ~120 ft/degC): ISA temp at 3,000 ft = 15 - (2x3) = 9 degC. At 35 degF (1.7 degC): deviation = 1.7-9 = -7.3 degC, DA = 3000 + 120x(-7.3) = ~2,120 ft. At 50 degF (10 degC): deviation = 10-9 = 1 degC, DA = 3000 + 120x1 = ~3,120 ft. Difference = ~1,000 ft increase, matching the chart reading.
